claim: William Hooper was one of North Carolina's three signers of the Declaration of Independence
source_quote: William Hooper — one of North Carolina's three signers

claim: William Hooper died at age forty-eight
source_quote: He died broke at forty-eight.

claim: William Hooper was born in Boston on 28 June 1742
source_quote: William Hooper was born in Boston on 28 June 1742, a child of the colonial elite.

claim: Hooper's father was a Scottish immigrant who became an Anglican (Church of England) minister
source_quote: His father, also William Hooper, was a Scottish immigrant who had risen to become an Anglican (Church of England) minister

claim: Hooper graduated from Harvard in 1760 at age eighteen
source_quote: Boston Latin School, then Harvard, where he graduated in 1760 at eighteen.

claim: Hooper read law under James Otis Jr.
source_quote: He read law under James Otis Jr.

claim: James Otis Jr. coined the phrase 'taxation without representation is tyranny'
source_quote: James Otis Jr., the firebrand whose phrase — "taxation without representation is tyranny" — would become the revolution's rallying cry.

claim: Hooper moved to North Carolina in 1764, first to Salisbury then Wilmington
source_quote: In 1764 Hooper moved south to North Carolina — first Salisbury, then the port town of Wilmington — to build a law practice.

claim: Hooper married Anne Clark and they had several children
source_quote: marriage to Anne Clark (they would have several children)

claim: Hooper's family estate was called Finian
source_quote: a fine house, and the estate the family called Finian.

claim: Hooper's father remained a staunch Loyalist when the break with Britain came
source_quote: The father — the Anglican minister, the man of the established church and the established crown — remained a staunch Loyalist.

claim: Hooper's father effectively disowned him due to his Patriot allegiance
source_quote: the elder Hooper, unable to reconcile his son's treason against the king he served, effectively disowned him.

claim: Hooper was elected to the North Carolina colonial assembly in 1773 representing Campbellton (later Fayetteville)
source_quote: Hooper was elected to the North Carolina colonial assembly in 1773 (representing Campbellton, later Fayetteville)

claim: Hooper was chosen in 1774 as one of North Carolina's three delegates to the Continental Congress
source_quote: chosen in 1774 as one of the colony's three delegates to the Continental Congress.

claim: Hooper signed the Continental Association in Philadelphia
source_quote: In Philadelphia he signed the Continental Association (the boycott of British goods)

claim: Hooper signed the Declaration of Independence in the summer of 1776
source_quote: and, in the summer of 1776, the Declaration of Independence.

claim: Signing the Declaration was legally tantamount to signing one's own death warrant if the rebellion failed
source_quote: To sign was, in legal reality, to sign his own death warrant if the rebellion failed — and everyone understood the British would hang traitors.

claim: Hooper poured his private wealth and future earnings into the Patriot cause
source_quote: He poured his private wealth and his future earnings into the Patriot cause, funding troops, supplies, and the machinery of rebellion out of his own pocket and credit.

claim: In early 1781 the British launched a major campaign into the Carolinas
source_quote: In early 1781, after years of the South being a secondary theatre, the British launched a major campaign into the Carolinas.

claim: British troops shelled and burned Hooper's estate at Finian when they occupied Wilmington
source_quote: Troops shelled and burned his estate at Finian and put his Wilmington home to the torch

claim: British forces destroyed two of Hooper's houses, his library, and his papers
source_quote: two houses gone, his library and papers destroyed, his land ravaged.

claim: Hooper became a fugitive for months, sheltered by sympathisers around Windsor and Edenton
source_quote: For months he slipped from house to house, sheltered by sympathisers, hiding in the countryside around Windsor and Edenton while British and Loyalist forces sought prominent rebels.

claim: Hooper was separated from his wife and young children for long stretches during the war
source_quote: He was separated from his wife and young children for long stretches, unable to return home, living on the run in a country whose independence he had declared but which was not yet won.

claim: The historical record confirms the burning of Hooper's home under the 1781 occupation and an extended period of displacement
source_quote: The historical record conservatively confirms the burning of his home under the 1781 occupation and an extended period of displacement

claim: Hooper survived the war and lived to see independence won
source_quote: Hooper survived the war. He lived to see independence won and the nation he had helped call into existence take its first uncertain steps.

claim: Hooper attempted to rebuild his law practice in the post-war depression but never regained his earlier prosperity
source_quote: He attempted to rebuild a law practice in the post-war depression, but the prosperity of the 1760s never returned.

claim: Hooper died on 14 October 1790 in Hillsborough, North Carolina, aged forty-eight
source_quote: He died on 14 October 1790 in Hillsborough, North Carolina, aged just forty-eight

claim: Hooper died only fourteen years after signing the Declaration of Independence
source_quote: only fourteen years after he had signed the document that pledged his life, his fortune, and his sacred honor.

claim: The Declaration's promise includes 'life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness'
source_quote: The Declaration's promise — "life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness" — reads as clean principle

claim: The biographical record confirms the Loyalist father, the Otis tutelage, the 1781 burning of his home, and the 1790 death at forty-eight
source_quote: History is verified here against the biographical record (the Loyalist father, the Otis tutelage, the 1781 burning of his home, the 1790 death at forty-eight)

claim: There were fifty-six signers of the Declaration of Independence
source_quote: fifty-six names, one bronze idea.

claim: Hooper traded his family, fortune, home, health, and almost his life for American independence
source_quote: William Hooper — one of North Carolina's three signers — traded his family, his fortune, his home, his health, and almost his life for a country he would barely live to see.

claim: Sovereignty is a balance sheet of sacrifice including family, fortune, home, health, and years
source_quote: Sovereignty, personal or national, is not a slogan or a bumper sticker. It is a balance sheet of sacrifice: family, fortune, home, health, years.

claim: Freedom is never free and those who declare it are the ones who pay for it
source_quote: freedom is never free — that the people who declare it are the ones who pay for it, and that remembering the price is part of keeping the inheritance.
